evidence.label: The hypercube Ramsey number has linear order

headline: Two-coloring the links among a constant times 2ⁿ points always gives a one-color n-dimensional cube, the paper claims.
scope: The result covers the two-color Ramsey number of the n-dimensional cube graph, for every n. The constant is absolute but not given as a number.
plain: The n-dimensional cube graph has 2ⁿ corners, linked when they differ in one coordinate. Color every link between M points red or blue, and ask how large M must be to force a one-color cube. Burr and Erdős asked in 1975 whether M can be a fixed constant times 2ⁿ. This paper claims to prove that it can, which settles the order of growth.
doesNot: This does not give a numerical value for the constant, or say what R(Qₙ)/2ⁿ tends to.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Stefan Burr and Paul Erdős, who posed the cube question
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a well-known question from 1975, with the best possible order of growth.

explanation:
Picture an ordinary cube. It has 8 corners and 12 edges. Label each corner by three digits, each 0 or 1, such as 010. Two corners share an edge exactly when their labels differ in one digit. Do the same with n digits and you get the n-dimensional cube graph Qₙ. It has 2ⁿ corners, and each corner has n links.

Now take M points and join every pair. Color each of these links red or blue. The Ramsey number R(Qₙ) is the smallest M that always leaves a one-color copy of the cube[1]. The copy may use extra links too; it only needs the cube's own links in one color.

Here is why M must be well above 2ⁿ. Take n = 3, and split 10 points into a block of 7 and a block of 3. Color links inside each block red, and links between blocks blue. A red cube would need 8 points inside one block, and the biggest has 7. A blue cube must put its two halves of 4 corners in opposite blocks, and one block has only 3[6]. So no one-color cube appears, and R(Q₃) is at least 11. In general this coloring shows R(Qₙ) is at least 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1[5].

In 1975 Burr and Erdős asked a sharper question. Is R(Qₙ) at most a fixed constant times 2ⁿ, for every n[2,3]? Cubes are a hard test case. Among families that could have this property, they have about as many links per corner as the known limit allows[4].

Related results came first. Graphs where every vertex has at most a fixed number of links have Ramsey numbers linear in their size, by a 1983 theorem[8]. Lee proved the same for a broader sparseness class in 2017[9]. Neither settles the cube, because each corner of Qₙ has n links, and n grows[10].

Bounds for the cube itself improved slowly. Write m = 2ⁿ for the number of corners. Shi showed in 2001 that R(Qₙ) is at most a fixed power of m[11]. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov got 2^(2n+6), which is 64m²[12]. Lee's work gives about m² plus n²m for large n[13]. Tikhomirov then pushed the power of m below 2[14]. For n = 10, the cube has 1,024 corners. The lower bound is 1,535, while Lee's upper bound is 1,150,976.

This paper claims that R(Qₙ) is at most C × 2ⁿ, with one absolute constant C, for every n[1]. That answers the Burr–Erdős question positively[18]. With the lower bound above, the order of growth is settled. The paper gives no number for C, and does not say what R(Qₙ)/2ⁿ approaches[7]. Earlier results for a cube against a fixed clique do not imply this one[15].

The single hard part is keeping the loss to a constant factor. The proof must handle colorings on only a slowly growing multiple of 2ⁿ points[16]. It assumes a coloring with no one-color cube in either color. From that it derives an imbalance in how the colors are spread, called discrepancy[17]. It then uses that imbalance to place the cube piece by piece.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. The constant C is not given as a number. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The graph whose vertices are all strings of n zeros and ones, linked when they differ in exactly one place.
The fewest points such that coloring every link among them red or blue always leaves a one-color copy of the graph H.

A sparseness measure: a graph is d-degenerate if every part of it has a vertex with at most d links.
